question: How could a good God punish anyone forever? Isn't the doctrine of hell itself the worst problem of evil?

ledger.heading: Seventeenth run (2026-11-20): an independent editor's read of the old-testament area, and the area "Evil, suffering and judgment"

objectionSource.author: Bertrand Russell
objectionSource.title: Why I Am Not a Christian

shortAnswer: This page weighs an argument; for someone afraid now, for themselves or for someone they love who has died, the pages on grief (/wisdom/grief) and on heaven and eternity (/wisdom/heaven-and-eternity), and Find Help (/help), are the better place to start, and nothing here speaks of any person's fate. All Christians confess that God will judge the world justly in Christ, that he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, and that salvation is in Christ alone. They differ on what final judgment is. Most of the church has held that the lost suffer conscious separation from God without end; many others hold that the finally impenitent at last perish; and a minority, outside most confessions, have hoped that all will in the end be restored. Each answers the moral objection at a different point, each has a real difficulty, and this page takes no side between the first two.

sections.heading: The objection at its strongest
sections.body:
Bertrand Russell put the charge plainly in a lecture in London in 1927, published as *Why I Am Not a Christian*. Jesus believed in hell, and Russell counted that against his character: "I do not myself feel that any person who is really profoundly humane can believe in everlasting punishment." He called the doctrine of hell-fire a doctrine of cruelty. Some sixty years earlier John Stuart Mill had refused, in his *Examination of Sir William Hamilton's Philosophy* (1865), to call any being good whose goodness was not what we mean by the word, and said that if such a being could send him to hell for refusing to call him good, to hell he would go.

As an argument, the objection is about proportion. A just punishment fits the wrong done. Every human life is finite, and even its worst wrongs are finite. Endless conscious suffering is infinite. So a God who punished that way would not be just. The objection is not only an unbeliever's. The philosopher Marilyn McCord Adams, herself a Christian, in her essay "The Problem of Hell: A Problem of Evil for Christians" (1993), asked, as the Stanford Encyclopedia's article on heaven and hell reports her question, how any sin committed by a finite creature, in a life of ambiguity, ignorance and illusion, could deserve an infinite penalty.

Dostoevsky gave the objection its sharpest human form. Ivan Karamazov, who has been describing cruelty done to children, refuses the idea that hell could set it right: "What good can hell do, since those children have already been tortured? And what becomes of harmony, if there is hell? I want to forgive. I want to embrace. I don't want more suffering" (in Constance Garnett's translation). At full strength the objection says that endless punishment adds suffering to a world already full of it, heals nothing, and makes the final state of God's creation contain an evil without end.

sections.heading: What is true in it
sections.body:
The church has sometimes preached hell with a relish that looks nothing like the Jesus who wept over Jerusalem, has used the fear of it to control people, and has spoken of the fate of others with a confidence Scripture doesn't give. Russell was right that a doctrine can make people cruel. And Adams was right that Christians can't answer the proportion argument by repeating the word "justice," since the argument is about what justice requires.

It should also be granted that Christians disagree, and have for a long time. The Study Bible's note on 2 Thessalonians 1 sets out two readings of "eternal destruction" side by side, and the site's argued answer on hell says the same. A reader who has been told that only one view has ever been held by serious Christians has been told something false.

sections.heading: The evidence
sections.body:
Begin with what all Christians confess, because it bears most of the weight. The Nicene Creed says that Christ "shall come again, with glory, to judge both the quick and the dead," the living and the dead. Scripture says that God "has set a day when He will judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed" (Acts 17:31, BSB); that the dead "were judged according to their deeds" (Revelation 20:12, BSB); and that God asks, "Do I take any pleasure in the death of the wicked? declares the Lord GOD. Wouldn't I prefer that he turn from his ways and live?" (Ezekiel 18:23, BSB). He "wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth" (1 Timothy 2:4, BSB), and "Salvation exists in no one else" (Acts 4:12, BSB). On these points the traditions agree.

The first view, held by most of the church through its history, is that the finally impenitent suffer conscious separation from God without end. Augustine taught it at length in *The City of God*, and the Reformation confessions state it plainly. The Lutheran Augsburg Confession says that Christ will condemn the ungodly "to be tormented without end," and the Westminster Confession that the wicked "shall be cast aside into eternal torments, and punished with everlasting destruction, from the presence of the Lord" (in the English of the copies read for this page). Its texts include Jesus' words, "they will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life" (Matthew 25:46, BSB), where one word describes both. Its holders answer the proportion argument by denying that sin is finite in the way it supposes. Thomas Aquinas argued that sin has two sides, an inordinate turning to a changeable good, which is finite, and a turning away from "the immutable good, which is infinite," so that its punishment, the loss of God, is infinite as well (*Summa Theologiae* I-II, q. 87, a. 4, in the English Dominican translation). C. S. Lewis gave a more human version in *The Problem of Pain* (1940): the damned, he wrote, are "rebels to the end," and "the doors of hell are locked on the inside." Its strongest difficulty is the one Adams pressed, the proportion between a finite creature's sin and an endless penalty, and with it two more: an endless suffering that heals no one, in a creation God says he will make new, and the question how a God who wants all to be saved keeps the lost in being forever.

The second view, called conditional immortality or annihilationism, holds that the finally impenitent are not kept alive in torment but at last perish. Its holders point out that Scripture says God "alone is immortal" (1 Timothy 6:16, BSB), that Jesus warned of "the One who can destroy both soul and body in hell" (Matthew 10:28, BSB), and that "the wages of sin is death" (Romans 6:23, BSB). The punishment is eternal in its result, not in endless suffering. Edward Fudge argued for it at length in *The Fire That Consumes* (1982). Its strongest difficulty is the text its opponents cite first: Matthew 25:46 sets "eternal punishment" beside "eternal life," and Revelation speaks of torment whose smoke "rises forever and ever" (Revelation 14:11, BSB). It must also answer that most of the church has read those words the other way.

The third view is the hope that God's love will in the end restore all. Origen in the third century wrote that "the end is always like the beginning" (*De Principiis* 1.6.2, in the Ante-Nicene Fathers translation), and Gregory of Nyssa held a hope of final restoration; in our time Thomas Talbott, a Christian philosopher, has argued for it in *The Inescapable Love of God*. Its holders point to God's purpose to "reconcile to Himself all things" (Colossians 1:20, BSB) and to the day when "God may be all in all" (1 Corinthians 15:28, BSB). The church's councils and most of its confessions have not received it. The Fifth General Council condemned the teaching of universal reconciliation in 553, and the Augsburg Confession expressly rejects the opinion that the punishments of the condemned will end. The Nicene and Apostles' Creeds don't define how long final punishment lasts, though the Athanasian Creed says that "they that have done evil" shall go "into everlasting fire"; those who hold the hope confess the Nicene faith, and they stand outside most of the church's confessions. Its strongest difficulty is Jesus' own warnings, which speak of no way back, among them the "great chasm" of his parable (Luke 16:26, BSB), and the question whether a love that will not finally accept a refusal respects the freedom of the one refusing.

sections.heading: The argument, laid out
sections.intro: This is an argument about what the moral objection shows: that judgment is not against God's goodness, and that the Christian accounts of hell each meet the proportion argument at a stated point.
steps: A good God can't treat grave wrongs as though they didn't matter, since that would treat their victims as though they didn't matter; many wrongs are never set right in this life; so a final judgment belongs to God's goodness rather than contradicting it.

The proportion argument against hell rests on three claims, that a just punishment fits the wrong, that every human wrong is finite, and that hell is endless conscious suffering, and each Christian account denies one of them on grounds drawn from Scripture and the church's reading of it: the traditional view the second, conditional immortality the third, and the hope of restoration the finality the argument assumes.
Each of these accounts is held by Christians who confess the creeds and the authority of Scripture, and each must carry texts and arguments it can't fully answer.
sections.conclusion: So: the moral objection doesn't show that a just and loving God can't judge; it shows where each account of hell's nature must give its answer, and why Christians who hold different accounts should hold them with care.
sections.after: The weight sits on the second step. If each denial were an evasion, invented to escape the argument rather than drawn from Scripture and the church's long reading of it, the objection would stand against all of them, and that is where it should be tested.

sections.heading: The strongest reply, and an answer
sections.body:
The strongest reply is Ivan's. Judgment may name the wrong, but endless punishment adds suffering to suffering and heals nothing, and a harmony built on it is not worth having. If God's purpose is to make all things new, a hell without end is a wound in the new creation itself.

The Christian answer begins by refusing a picture the reply assumes, that hell is God's pleasure in pain. It is not; he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked. Judgment, on the Christian account, is first the truth told: the victims named, the wrong called wrong, and evil ended. And it is borne by God before it falls on anyone. Paul writes that God set forth Christ "so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus" (Romans 3:26, BSB). Alyosha's answer to Ivan, in the same chapter of the novel, is that there is "a Being and He can forgive everything, all and for all, because He gave His innocent blood for all and everything." Whatever hell is, on every Christian account it is not God's pleasure, and on many it is what remains when a person finally refuses what God has given at that cost. That doesn't remove the difficulty each view carries, and this page has named them. It does mean that the objection, aimed at a God who delights in pain, misses the God Christians confess; aimed at endless punishment itself, it presses the difficulty the traditional view has already been asked to carry.

A reader who is afraid, for himself or for someone he loves who has died, should hear what every Christian tradition confesses before any of this. Judgment belongs to Christ, to whom "the Father ... has assigned all judgment" (John 5:22, BSB), the one who wept over Jerusalem and said, "the one who comes to Me I will never drive away" (John 6:37, BSB). No page, preacher or tradition knows the heart of another person at the end, and this one will not guess. Abraham's question still stands for every grieving believer: "Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?" (Genesis 18:25, BSB). A pastor, and Find Help (/help), are there for anyone who needs to talk about this now.

sections.heading: What remains unresolved
sections.body: What hell is, and how long it lasts, is unresolved among faithful Christians, and the site takes no side between eternal conscious punishment and conditional immortality. How the joy of the redeemed fits with the loss of others is a question no view fully answers. How God's will that all be saved and the freedom to refuse him finally fit together is answered differently by the Augustinian, Arminian and other traditions. And who will be lost is not known to anyone, and Christians who speak as if they know it claim what Jesus never gave them.

sections.heading: Where Christians differ
sections.body:
Christians differ on the nature and duration of final punishment, as the evidence above sets out. The historic confessions that speak to it, the Augsburg and Westminster among them, teach eternal conscious punishment; a number of evangelical scholars and pastors, Fudge among them, have held conditional immortality; and a smaller number hope for universal restoration, a view most confessions reject. The site takes no side between the first two, and it states the third as the church has generally judged it, as a hope outside its confessions, without contempt for those who hold it.

What all confess is the floor: Christ will come to judge the living and the dead; the judgment will be just; God takes no pleasure in anyone's death; salvation is by grace, in Christ alone; and the life of the world to come is real.
